Imagine that after years of struggling to have a child, you finally achieve your dream through in vitro fertilisation. Your joy is overwhelming, but there is something you may not immediately think about. Several embryos created during your IVF treatment may still be frozen in a laboratory, waiting for a decision about their future. Perhaps you intend to return for another child, or perhaps you have already had the number of children you want; you may even have changed your mind about having another pregnancy. Whatever your circumstances, those embryos remain in storage, and someone must eventually decide what happens to them. This is one of the less discussed consequences of modern fertility treatment. While much attention is given to the success of IVF, the fate of embryos that are never transferred is often overlooked. When you begin IVF, your immediate concern is understandably getting pregnant. You may not want to imagine a situation in which you have more embryos than you need, or find yourself making decisions about them years after your treatment. Yet that is precisely the dilemma confronting many couples who undergo assisted reproductive treatment. During IVF, eggs retrieved from your ovaries are fertilised with sperm in a laboratory. Depending on the number of eggs collected and the success of fertilisation, several embryos may develop. Your fertility specialist may recommend transferring one or two embryos at a time; other suitable embryos can be preserved through cryopreservation for future use. The process commonly involves vitrification, a rapid freezing technique that protects embryos from the formation of damaging ice crystals. They are stored in specialised tanks containing liquid nitrogen at temperatures of approximately minus 196 degrees Celsius. The technology has transformed fertility treatment. If your first IVF attempt does not succeed, you may have another opportunity without undergoing the entire process of ovarian stimulation and egg retrieval again. If you achieve pregnancy and later decide to have another child, your frozen embryos may provide another option. But what happens when you no longer need them? You may have had two children and decided your family is complete, and suddenly, embryos that once represented hope become a difficult responsibility. You may be surprised to discover that freezing embryos is only the beginning of a longer commitment. They must remain in carefully monitored storage facilities, and this comes at a cost. Once your immediate reproductive needs have been met, continuing to pay storage fees may no longer appear financially necessary. But failing to renew your storage agreement does not automatically resolve the fate of your embryos. This is how embryos can become what are commonly described as abandoned embryos. It does not always mean that you deliberately walked away from them. Sometimes, it reflects financial difficulties, changing circumstances, poor communication or disagreement between partners. The situation becomes more complicated when you and your partner no longer agree about what should happen. You may want to preserve the embryos because you still hope to have another child. Your partner may feel that your family is complete and refuse to continue storage. One of you may want the embryos donated to another couple, while the other may prefer their disposal. Consent is central to embryo cryopreservation. Before treatment, you and your partner should be required to indicate what should happen to the embryos under different circumstances, including separation, divorce, death or a decision not to have more children. These agreements are important because embryos involve the reproductive interests of both people who provided the genetic material. You may have changed your mind about having another child. Your partner may still want to proceed, but the fact that you previously agreed to create and freeze embryos does not necessarily mean that either person can unilaterally decide to use them later. Consent to storage and consent to reproductive use are not necessarily the same thing. For some couples, donating unused embryos to another person or couple may provide a way forward. If you choose embryo donation, your remaining embryos may offer another family an opportunity to have a child. This can be particularly meaningful for people who cannot produce viable eggs or sperm, or who have experienced repeated IVF failures. There are questions about donor confidentiality, genetic identity, medical history and whether children born through embryo donation should have access to information about their biological origins. In Nigeria, where cultural expectations, family relationships and religious beliefs strongly influence reproductive decisions, these conversations can be particularly sensitive. You may find the idea of another family raising a child genetically related to you unacceptable. Your religious convictions may also influence your decision. Another couple, however, may see embryo donation as an opportunity to help someone experience parenthood. Whatever your position, donation should be voluntary and based on informed consent, proper counselling and appropriate safeguards. Then, what happens when you neither want to use nor donate your remaining embryos? Disposal may become the only option you are willing to consider. This may be a straightforward decision, or it can trigger emotional and moral conflict. Your beliefs about when human life begins may influence how you view embryos outside the womb. Without agreement, embryos may remain in storage for years, leaving fertility clinics with difficult decisions about their management. For Nigeria’s growing fertility industry, this is an issue that deserves greater attention. As more Nigerians embrace IVF and other assisted reproductive technologies, questions about the management of unused embryos are becoming increasingly relevant. How many frozen embryos are currently held in fertility clinics? Questions raise concerns about consent, storage agreements, record-keeping, confidentiality and the responsibilities of fertility centres. If you are considering IVF, you should not wait until you have achieved pregnancy before discussing what happens to embryos that remain unused. You need to understand the storage fees, renewal arrangements, withdrawal of consent, donation options and the clinic’s policy when patients cannot be contacted. Ultimately, frozen embryos are more than laboratory material. They are connected to your hopes of becoming a parent, your relationships, your beliefs and the decisions you make about your family. You may initially see them as an insurance against another unsuccessful IVF attempt or an opportunity to have another child. But years later, you may find yourself confronting a decision you never expected to make. Cryopreservation can preserve your reproductive possibilities, sometimes for many years. It cannot, however, determine what you should do with those possibilities. Abayomi Ajayi
